Prevention: Tie a clear (see- through) plastic bag over the okra pods.
This stops the cotton stainers from feeding on the pods.
Uproot and burn all volunteer okra plants and stubbles after harvest
Bury the uprooted cotton and debris at least 0.5 m deep
Apply compost, the compost heat will kill the developing strainers in soil debris
Do not allow alternative host plants such as cotton and pepper in and around the okra field
Monitoring: Adult stainers have brown and black backs with two black spots with red and white stripes underneath the body.
Young stainers have red and white stripes all over the body.
These insects may feed for several days on okra plants, leaving black spots on the dry pods.
Start monitoring for stainers at 50% flowering up to pod maturity
Check plants in field for stainers during the flowering and fruiting period.
Monitor populations by counting number of stainers per plant
Look for stainers underneath the leaves, observe for sucking punctures and stains on leaves and fruits
If about 5-10 stainers are observed in a sample size of 20 plants, initiate control measures.
Additional relevant crops: pepper, tomato, cotton and akee apple
Direct Control: Remove stainers on okro leaves and place into a container of water with a thin flim of kerosene to reduce late season populations
Spray infested okro plants with extract consisting of 15g/L of dried neem seed, add 2g of potassium soap (20%), add hot pepper (1 margarine tin).
Spray every 10 days from seedling until flowering.
Restrictions: When using a pesticide or botanical, always wear protective clothing and follow the instructions on the product label.
Do not use chemicals with the same mode of action year after year as this can lead to resistance.
